content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) established the Vessel Sanitation Program (VSP) in 1975 in collaboration with the cruise vessel industry. The primary objective of the VSP is to assist the cruise industry in developing and implementing comprehensive sanitation programs to safeguard the health of passengers and crew aboard cruise ships. Cruise vessels docking at U.S. ports undergo biannual operational inspections and, if necessary, re-inspections conducted by the VSP. The vessel owner is required to pay a fee for these inspections, which is determined based on the gross registered tonnage (GRT) of the vessel. Additionally, cruise vessel owners or shipyards involved in the construction or renovation of cruise ships may voluntarily request plan reviews, on-site shipyard construction inspections, and final construction inspections before the vessel's first or next operational inspection. Fees for on-site and final construction inspections are also based on the vessel's GRT, but no fees are charged for plan reviews or consultations. The guidelines provided by the VSP, referred to as the Vessel Sanitation Program Construction Manual, aim to establish consistent construction and design standards that protect the health of passengers and crew. Compliance with these guidelines ensures a healthy environment on cruise vessels. The CDC developed these guidelines by reviewing numerous references from various sources and is committed to promoting high construction standards to protect public health. The guidelines cover various aspects of a vessel's facilities related to public health, including food storage, preparation, and service; water bunkering, storage, disinfection, and distribution. Vessel owners and operators have the flexibility to select designs and equipment that meet their needs, provided they comply with the sanitary design criteria of the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) or equivalent organizations, as well as the VSP's operational inspection requirements. These guidelines do not restrict the introduction of new designs, materials, or technologies in shipbuilding. Shipbuilders, owners, manufacturers, or other interested parties may request periodic reviews or revisions of the guidelines to incorporate new information or technology. The guidelines also align with international maritime conventions, such as the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS) Convention, the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL), and others. However, the document does not cross-reference related or overlapping standards that new cruise vessels must meet. The guidelines became effective on June 1, 2005, and apply to all structural changes made to vessels after this date. Minor renovations, such as the installation or removal of single pieces of equipment or single pipe runs, are excluded. The guidelines apply to all areas of the vessel affected by a renovation, and the VSP inspects the entire vessel during routine sanitation inspections and re-inspections. The VSP periodically reviews and revises its recommendations in collaboration with industry representatives and other stakeholders to keep pace with industry innovations. Shipbuilders, owners, manufacturers, or other interested parties may request the VSP to review a construction guideline based on new technologies, concepts, or methods. Requests should identify the section to be revised, describe the proposed change or addition, state the reason for the recommendation, and include supporting research or test results. To request plan reviews, consultations, or construction-related inspections, an official written request must be submitted to the VSP Chief as early as possible during the planning, construction, or renovation process. Requests requiring foreign travel must be submitted at least 60 days before the intended visit. The VSP assigns primary and secondary officers to coordinate with the vessel owner and shipyard, serving as points of contact throughout the process. Vessel representatives should also designate points of contact to represent the owners, shipyard, and key subcontractors. Plan reviews for new construction are typically conducted 18-24 months before the vessel's scheduled delivery, while the timeline for major renovations varies. Plan reviews usually take two working days and are conducted in Atlanta, Georgia; Fort Lauderdale, Florida; or other agreed-upon locations. Representatives from the shipyard, vessel owner, and subcontractors should attend the review and bring all relevant plans, drawings, and equipment specifications. The VSP prepares a Plan Review Report summarizing recommendations and submits it to the shipyard and owner representatives. Following the review, the shipyard must provide a complete set of plans, any redrawn plans, a statement of corrective action, and copies of any major change orders. During construction, shipyard representatives, owners, or other vessel representatives may direct questions or requests for consultative services to the VSP project officers. These inquiries should be submitted in writing, including fax numbers and email addresses for appropriate contacts. The VSP officers coordinate the request with the designated points of contact. On-site construction inspections are typically conducted in shipyards outside the United States. Shipyards are encouraged to contact the VSP Chief well in advance of the 60-day minimum to better plan inspection dates. On-site inspections generally require one to three officers, depending on the vessel's size and whether it is the first of a hull design class or a subsequent hull in the same class. Inspections, including travel, usually take five working days and should be conducted approximately 4-5 weeks before the vessel's delivery when 90% of the areas to be inspected are completed. The VSP provides a written report to the requesting party, and the shipyard must submit a statement of corrective action before the ship's arrival in the United States. At the request of a vessel owner or shipyard, the VSP may conduct a final construction inspection. To schedule this inspection, a formal written request must be submitted to the VSP Chief as soon as possible after the vessel is completed or at least 10 days before its arrival in the United States. If a final construction inspection is not requested, the VSP will generally conduct an unannounced operational inspection within four weeks of the vessel's arrival. Following the final construction inspection, the vessel owner or shipyard must submit a statement of corrective action outlining how they will address each item cited in the inspection report, including the projected completion date. The VSP establishes certain standards for equipment and materials installed on cruise vessels but does not test, certify, or endorse any equipment or materials. Instead, the VSP recognizes certifications from independent testing laboratories such as NSF International, Underwriters Laboratories (UL), and ANSI. Equipment built to questionable standards is reviewed by a committee comprising VSP, cruise ship industry, and independent testing organization participants to determine compliance with the recommended standards. Equipment manufacturers and suppliers should not refer to VSP for product approval. The guidelines also provide definitions for various terms related to vessel sanitation, such as accessible, air-gap, backflow, black water, gray water, and others. These definitions ensure clarity and consistency in the application of the guidelines. Additionally, the guidelines outline general facility requirements, including the size and flow of rooms and work areas, which must accommodate the vessel's full capacity of passengers and crew. Refrigeration and hot-food holding facilities must also be available for all food preparation and service operations.
